content: Rapid diagnostic tests for HIV serology are recommended for diagnosing HIV in children older than 18 months, following national testing strategies. To improve the accuracy of nucleic acid-based early infant diagnosis assays, an indeterminate range of viral copy equivalents should be used. National regulatory agencies are encouraged to adopt point-of-care early infant diagnosis without unnecessary delays, streamlining registration and approval processes for immediate implementation. Biological children of parents living with HIV or who may have died from HIV should be routinely offered HIV testing services. If found to be infected or at high risk of infection, they should be linked to treatment or prevention services and provided with a comprehensive package of voluntary, provider-assisted referrals. HIV testing services for adolescents, particularly those from key populations, are recommended, with linkages to prevention, treatment, and care. Adolescents should be counseled on the benefits and risks of disclosing their HIV-positive status and supported in deciding whether, when, how, and to whom to disclose this information. In high HIV burden settings, HIV testing services with linkages to prevention, treatment, and care are recommended for all adolescents. In low HIV burden settings, these services should be accessible to adolescents in low and concentrated epidemic areas. HIV testing services should be routinely offered to all key populations in both community and facility-based settings. Community-based HIV testing, with linkages to prevention, treatment, and care, should complement facility-based testing. Social network-based approaches may also be offered as part of a comprehensive care and prevention package for key populations. All pregnant women should be tested for HIV, syphilis, and hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) at least once and as early as possible during pregnancy. Dual HIV and syphilis rapid diagnostic tests can be used as the first test in HIV testing strategies during antenatal care. Provider-assisted referral should be offered to all people with HIV as part of a voluntary, comprehensive package of testing and care. Women disclosing violence by an intimate partner or sexual assault should be offered immediate support, including first-line support from healthcare providers or referral to accessible services. Mandatory or coercive HIV testing is never justified. Providers should assess the risk of harm and determine the most appropriate approach for couple and partner testing, including supportive options like provider assistance, while avoiding testing in inadvisable situations. Lay providers trained and supervised to use rapid diagnostic tests can independently conduct safe and effective HIV testing services. Western blotting and line immunoassays should not be used in national HIV testing strategies and algorithms. HIV testing algorithms should achieve at least 99% positive predictive value and use tests with high sensitivity and specificity. Countries should consider a three-test strategy as HIV positivity rates fall below 5% in national programs. Retesting is recommended for all individuals newly diagnosed with HIV before initiating antiretroviral therapy (ART) to verify their status. Retesting is not recommended for individuals already on ART, as it may yield incorrect results. Nucleic acid testing (NAT) at birth can be added to existing early infant diagnosis approaches to identify HIV infection in exposed infants. Point-of-care nucleic acid testing is recommended for diagnosing HIV in infants and children younger than 18 months. The correct and consistent use of condoms with compatible lubricants is recommended for all key populations to prevent sexual transmission of HIV and sexually transmitted infections (STIs). Individuals who inject drugs should have access to sterile injecting equipment through needle and syringe programs. Opioid substitution therapy should be offered to people dependent on opioids, including those in prisons or closed settings. Evidence-based interventions, including brief psychosocial interventions, should be accessible to key populations with harmful alcohol or substance use. Naloxone should be available to individuals likely to witness an opioid overdose, with instructions for emergency use. Voluntary medical male circumcision (VMMC) should continue to be promoted as an effective HIV prevention option for adolescent boys aged 15 years and older and adult men in settings with generalized epidemics. WHO-prequalified male circumcision devices are recommended as additional methods for HIV prevention in males aged 15 years and older. The dapivirine vaginal ring may be offered as an additional prevention option for cisgender women at substantial risk of HIV infection. TDF + 3TC (or FTC) is recommended as the preferred backbone regimen for HIV PEP in adults and adolescents, with dolutegravir (DTG) as the preferred third drug. For children aged 10 years and younger, AZT + 3TC is the preferred backbone regimen for HIV PEP, with DTG as the preferred third drug when approved dosing is available. Infants born to mothers with HIV at high risk of acquiring HIV should receive dual prophylaxis with daily AZT and NVP for the first six weeks of life. Breastfed infants at high risk should continue prophylaxis for an additional six weeks, totaling 12 weeks. ART should be initiated for all people living with HIV regardless of clinical stage or CD4 cell count. Rapid ART initiation, defined as within seven days of diagnosis, should be offered to all individuals following a confirmed HIV diagnosis and clinical assessment. Same-day ART initiation should be offered to those ready to start. ART initiation should follow principles of people-centered care, respecting individual dignity and preferences. Immediate ART initiation is not recommended for individuals with cryptococcal meningitis due to increased mortality risk and should be deferred by 4–6 weeks after starting antifungal treatment. ART should be initiated as soon as possible for individuals with disseminated histoplasmosis without central nervous system involvement. DTG-based regimens are preferred for first-line ART in adults, adolescents, and children with approved dosing. In settings where DTG is inaccessible or unsuitable, PI/r-based regimens should be used. EFV at a low dose (400 mg) is recommended as an alternative first-line regimen for adults and adolescents initiating ART in settings with low NNRTI resistance. For neonates, RAL-based regimens may be recommended as the preferred first-line option. DTG in combination with an optimized NRTI backbone is preferred for second-line ART in individuals failing non-DTG-based regimens. Boosted protease inhibitors with an optimized NRTI backbone are recommended for individuals failing DTG-based regimens. National programs should develop policies for third-line ART, including new drugs with minimal cross-resistance to previously used regimens. Viral load testing is the preferred approach for monitoring ART response and diagnosing treatment failure. Routine viral load monitoring should be conducted at six months, 12 months, and annually thereafter. CD4 cell count monitoring can be stopped for individuals established on ART in settings with routine viral load monitoring. In settings without routine viral load testing, CD4 count and clinical monitoring should be used to diagnose treatment failure. Dried blood spot specimens can be used for viral load testing when logistical barriers prevent plasma specimen testing. For individuals initiating first-line ART with pretreatment NNRTI resistance, NNRTI-containing regimens should be avoided. A package of interventions, including screening, treatment, and/or prophylaxis for opportunistic infections, rapid ART initiation, and adherence support, should be offered to individuals with advanced HIV disease. Screening for cryptococcal antigen followed by pre-emptive antifungal therapy is recommended to prevent invasive cryptococcal disease before initiating or restarting ART.
